references.text: The preceding context establishes the laws concerning an ox that gores people, including free persons. Verse 32 extends this law to apply to slaves.
The laws regarding slaves and bondmen in Israel provide background for why there were specific rules for compensation when a slave was killed.
Zechariah mentions thirty pieces of silver as the price at which he was valued, the same sum as the compensation for a slave in Exodus 21:32.
Judas receives thirty pieces of silver to betray Jesus, an amount that echoes the value of a slave in Exodus 21:32 and Zechariah's prophecy.
Matthew explicitly links the thirty pieces of silver to the prophecy and the price of a slave, showing the fulfillment of this symbolic sum.
Both verses form a coherent legal framework concerning an owner's liability for fatal injury to bondmen, whether through direct violence or animal damage.
Complementary rules within the same law code: 21:32 regulates death (compensation), while 21:26 regulates permanent injury (freedom) to protect the integrity of the bondman.
Confirmation of the standard value for a woman (30 shekels) used both in damage compensation and for vow offerings.
